extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media scholars, and media-industry professionals interested in journalistic standards and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and evaluate journalistic practices and standards (objectivity, transparency, audience, and the role of information) as exemplified by sites like TechCrunch. Useful for assessing ethics, public interest obligations, and business-model impacts on journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency is the new objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: For transparency advocates, the formula is simple. True objectivity is impossible. All communicators enter a larger communicative space with particular biases and conflicts of interest. Therefore, rather than claiming objectivity, it is better for journalists to be transparent about what these biases are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether journalists and outlets disclose relevant biases, relationships, and conflicts of interest. The page uses TechCrunch as an example: investment in startups covered is acceptable 'as long as he is transparent about this fact.' Treat transparency as a primary evaluative dimension, but do not assume it fully substitutes for other ethical safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity (traditional journalistic ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity is an ideal that many view as impossible but still 'worth striving for anyway' as a professional standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider objectivity as a benchmark for methods (balanced sourcing, separation of reporting and opinion), while recognizing critiques that the ideal is strained in contemporary media; weigh how claims of objectivity interact with transparency and audience orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'it is fine for Michael Arrington to invest in startups that his website covers, as long as he is transparent about this fact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether conflicts (financial, personal, institutional) are explicitly disclosed to readers. Failure to disclose is a clear ethical lapse; disclosure is expected, especially when coverage could influence markets or decisions (e.g., investment cues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure can have perverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral-economics research (Cain, Loewenstein, Moore) shows disclosure may fail to solve problems created by conflicts of interest and 'may sometimes even make matters worse.' Disclosure can increase bias because it leads advisors to feel morally licensed and strategically encouraged to exaggerate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating disclosure, account for possible downstream effects: disclosed conflicts do not guarantee informed reader judgment and may enable more aggressive framing by the source. Consider additional safeguards beyond disclosure (editorial checks, separation of duties, explicit standards on participation in markets covered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-serving versus client-serving orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism may be defined by an attitude toward the public — for the professional journalist, the public is her client. Industry newsletters serve members of a trade who need information for strategic decisions. A 'public' consists of those affected by indirect consequences of transactions (John Dewey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an outlet aims to serve a broad public interest (public consequences, accountability) or a narrower client/audience (industry insiders, investors). Scrutinize claims that an outlet 'serves the public' against its actual audience, beats, resources, and where it directs attention and investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry newsletter function and public consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: TechCrunch often fits the model of an industry newsletter — focused on the ins and outs of one field, 'unafraid of being too inside baseball' — but sometimes covers issues with public consequences, which complicates how it's characterized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an industry-focused publication covers matters with wider public impact, evaluate whether it applies broader journalistic responsibilities (verification, consideration of public harms/benefits) rather than only serving trade needs. Distinguish routine trade reporting from reporting that implicates public policy or welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fetishizing information / Information as sole criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: MG Siegler: 'But ultimately there is only one thing that matters: information. People don’t care how they get it, just that they get it. ... Information is all that matters. All the rest is bullshit.' Under this view, success is measured by distribution (pageviews, CPMs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an outlet treats the provision of information (speed, quantity, accessibility) as the primary or sole measure of success. Consider market metrics (pageviews, ad revenue) versus journalistic quality indicators (verification, context, impact). Beware of equating distribution metrics with journalistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism's purposes beyond information (knowledge, wisdom, truth, beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterpoint: 'Information is not knowledge. Knowledge is not wisdom. Wisdom is not truth. Truth is not beauty. Beauty is not love. Love is not music. Music is THE BEST.' This suggests journalism might aim for more than raw information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether journalists aim to produce deeper understanding, context, accountability, and public goods beyond merely supplying information. Consider criteria such as explanatory depth, investigative rigor, ethical framing, and contributions to public deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience identification and impact orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: TechCrunch primarily serves 'a certain subset of plugged in Silicon Valley obsessives and investors' yet covers topics with broader public consequences; the identity of who is being served matters for how journalism is judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who the intended and actual audiences are (investors, insiders, general public) and how that orientation shapes coverage choices, sourcing, framing, and ethical obligations. An outlet's audience profile should inform expectations about balance, depth, and accountability.
